newsitem.title: POLAND: FOREIGNERS SEEN FLOCKING BACK TO ZLOTY NEXT WEEK.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGNERS SEEN FLOCKING BACK TO ZLOTY NEXT WEEK.

text.p: Foreign investors are expected to flock back to high yielding zloty-denominated papers next week after a brief but heavy-handed withdrawal over the past days pushed the zloty down to its lowest levels ever, analysts said.

Foreign investors, either covering losses caused by the Czech crown's sharp fall or cutting Central European currency exposure in general, pulled out some $400 million from Poland over the last week, sinking the zloty more than two percent.
But on Thursday and Friday the zloty regained initiative and charged upward, backed by bullish statements from Poland's Finance Minister and renewed foreign interest in Polish papers.

"After several weeks of minimal interest, foreign investors are likely to again show up in force at Monday's T-bill tender ...(and) put the zloty under upward pressure next week," said Wlodzimierz Kado, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Analysts said, however, that the zloty's upward push would probably meet National Bank of Poland interventions against it, after the central bank bought currencies on Friday when the zloty strengthened above 1.5 percent from parity.

"Today's intervention showed the NBP believes 1.5 percent would be a good resistance, but it may well have to repeat its currency-buying in order to enforce this level," said Mateusz Bieniek, foreign exchange dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.

Some other dealers said the central bank's intervention at 1.5 percent from parity may have been made simply to cool the zloty, which soared more than one percent against the basket in several hours of trading, not to establish new resistance.
On Friday, the NBP bought some $20 million between 1.62 and 1.47 percent from the parity rate, capping the zloty's gains.
The zloty closed the week at 1.53/1.47 percent from the parity rate, up from last Friday's close at 0.64/0.50 percent.
It briefly sank on Tuesday to an all-time low against the basket, level with parity, as the Czech crown tumbled some seven to eight percent amid foreign investor withdrawal.

Analysts said that more upbeat Polish fundamentals, such as steady economic growth created by largely restructured industry, and tighter regulations over capital markets, kept the zloty from plunging in line with its Czech neighbour.
At Monday's 1.6 billion zloty primary T-bill auction yields are likely to hold unchanged or edge upward, dealers said.
"Yields should remain on the same level, or nudge upward on the longest bills, as the treasury increased its offer," said Marta Kepa, dealer at Pekao SA.
The maximum yield of the benchmark 52-week T-bill was expected to be around 21.48 percent, against a 21.40 percent average yield at Monday's tender.
Yields of 26-week, 13-week and eight-week papers were expected to hold steady around 21.34, 20.87 and 20.77 percent.

Dealers said that even though the recent foreign sales had absorbed some demand from domestic corporates, Polish banks were still likely to bid for large amounts of bills on Monday, as a new monthly reserve period pulled down one-day rates.
"Costs of financing will probably drop next week as a new monthly reserve period begins, so banks may try to buy bills for their trading portfolios," said Robert Gluch, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.
